title: Chapter 61: The Free Valleys, Part 2 of 5: The Drove Road
html:
The road went up the valley, and they went with it.
It was a long valley, and a lonely one. A small stream ran down the bottom of it, half frozen, talking to itself under a lid of ice. The road ran beside the stream, a little above it, between its two gray walls. The walls were made of flat stones piled one on another with nothing to hold them but their own weight. Nobody had used mortar. Nobody had needed to. The stones had been sitting on each other for so long that they had grown together, and moss had grown over all of them, a thick green-gray moss, soft as fur, with a white cap of snow along the top of the wall like icing on a long cake.
There were trees, now and then. Not many. Hawthorns, mostly, small and black and twisted, growing out of the wall itself, as if somebody had planted them there to hold it up. Every one of them leaned the same way. Every branch on every tree was bent hard over toward the south, toward the fens and the city, as if a great hand had pushed them all down in the same direction and held them there for a hundred years.
"Wind," said Oren, when Corin asked. "It comes down off the hills from the north, every day of the year. Bends them." He looked at one of the little trees with his head on one side. "Or else they're trying to get away from something."
He said it like a joke. Nobody laughed.
The sun came up properly at last, round and white behind the thin cloud, and for an hour the snow on the hills went the color of the inside of a shell, pink and gold, and then went white again. Their shadows lay long and blue on the road in front of them. Corin's shadow had three legs. He watched it swing along. Crutch and bad leg, good leg.
Oren dropped back to walk beside him.
He did it without saying anything. One moment he was out ahead, and the next he had slowed and let Corin come up level with him, and they were walking side by side, the big soldier with his arm in a sling and the gray-handed man with his crutch, like two old men coming home from a fair.
"You've walked a lot of these," said Corin.
"Some." Oren looked up at the hills. "In the war. When I was young. The Commonwealth Foot. They used to march us on the drove roads when they wanted to move us quiet, because the walls keep you low." He held his good hand out flat, at the height of the wall. "See? You're down below the top of the land. Off the skyline. A man on that hill there could look straight down this valley and not see a whole company walking up it, if they kept their heads down and their mouths shut."
"Did you keep your mouth shut?"
"Never." Oren's beard moved. "The sergeant used to say I talked like a—" He stopped.
Corin waited.
Oren's face had gone still and careful. Corin had seen that look before, many times now. It was the look of a man reaching for a word on a shelf and finding the shelf empty.
"Like a—the thing. In a kitchen." Oren moved his good hand in a small circle. "You hang it over the fire. You put the water in it. It shouts when it's ready."
"A kettle."
"A kettle." Oren let out his breath. "Aye. That's still there, then. Good." He walked a few steps. "I never know, till I reach for one, which ones are still there. You'd think a man would know what's in his own head."
Corin did not say anything for a while. Then he said, "I know."
"Aye," said Oren. "You would."
They walked.
Up ahead, the girl had stopped by a place where the wall had fallen down, and she was looking through the gap at something on the hillside. A hare, Corin saw, when he came up. A brown hare, sitting up on its back legs in the snow, with its long ears straight up, not running. It looked at them. Then it turned and went away up the hill in long, easy, loping jumps, as if it had all the time in the world.
The girl watched it until it was gone. Then she went on, without a word to either of them.
Oren watched her go.
"She's not angry with you," he said.
Corin looked at him.
"I know what it looks like." Oren rubbed his beard. "She walks out ahead, and she won't look at you, and when she does she looks like she's going to bite. I know. I've known her since she was born. I know what it looks like." He shook his head. "She's not angry. She's—" He reached for the word, and this time it was there. "She's grieving. Her father died last night, and she held his hand while he did it. And you—" He stopped.
"And I don't know her."
"And you don't know her. And she knows you. All of you. Every bit, from the first day." Oren walked a few steps. "I had a mate in the war, lost his sight in a cannon flash. Afterward he used to say the worst of it wasn't the dark. It was everybody else being able to see him, when he couldn't see them. Like being the only one in a room with no candle." He glanced sideways at Corin. "She's the one in the room with the candle, and you're the one in the dark, and she's got to watch you feel your way along the walls. That's what it is. That's all."
Corin thought about that for a long time.
"What should I do?" he said.
Oren laughed. It was a short, rough, surprised sound, like a dog barking once.
"Saints, man. How would I know? I'm a soldier." He shook his head. "Ask her things. You're doing that. That's good. And when she won't answer, let her not answer. You're doing that too." He paused. "And don't ever, ever tell her she sings flat. Even if she does."
"She told me I'd said that."
"Aye, you did. In the crypt. With your leg open." Oren's mouth twitched. "She's never forgiven you."
They came round a bend of the valley, and the wind found them.
It came straight down the valley from the north, from between the hills, and it was colder than anything Corin had felt in the fens. It went through the black wool of his coat as if the coat were not there. It went through his skin. It made his eyes run and his teeth ache. On his left cheek it was so cold that after a while he could not feel the cheek at all, and he put up his gloved hand to it, to see if it was still there.
Under the wind, very faint, there was something else.
He stopped.
Oren stopped beside him. "What?"
"Listen."
They listened. The wind roared softly in their ears. The stream talked under its ice. Somewhere up the hill a sheep called, a thin flat sound.
And under all of it, so low that it was less a sound than a feeling, something hummed.
It was one note. One long, low, steady note, too low to hear properly, like the lowest string of some huge instrument being drawn on very slowly, a long way off. He felt it in his back teeth before he heard it in his ears. He felt it in the bones of his face.
Oren frowned. "I don't hear anything."
"Put your teeth together."
Oren looked at him as if he had gone mad. Then he did it. His frown changed.
"Saints," he said quietly. "What is that?"
That, said Malakor, from very far away inside Corin's head, so faint that Corin had to hold his breath to hear him, is the Glass. Singing. It does that. It's been doing it for sixty years. A pause. You'll get used to it, boy. Everybody does. In the end you stop hearing it at all, and then one day you go away from it, and the quiet is so loud you can't sleep.
You've been there.
Walk, said Malakor. We're nearly at the fork.
Corin had not known there was a fork.
He did not ask how Malakor knew. He put his crutch forward, and his bad leg, and swung his good leg past, and went on up the road into the wind, and the hum went with him, low and steady in his teeth, like a cat purring somewhere in the walls of a house.
The Two Sisters
The fork was at the head of the valley, where two streams came down from two different hills and met.
The road split there. One way went right, up the eastern stream, a broad way between walls that were high and well kept, with fresh stones put back in the gaps and the snow on it trodden down by many feet and wheels. The other way went left, up the western stream. It was narrower. Its walls were lower and older, green almost to the top with moss, fallen down in places, so that the snow had drifted over the road and nobody had trodden it flat. It looked as if nobody had gone that way all winter.
In the angle between the two roads stood the Two Sisters.
That was what they were called. Corin did not know how he knew that. He would think about that later. At the time he only looked at them and the name was there, as plain as his own.
They were cairns. Two tall heaps of piled stone, each of them as tall as two men, standing side by side in the angle of the fork. They were not straight. They leaned in toward each other at the top, so that there was only a hand's width of sky between them, like two old women bending their heads together to tell a secret. One of them had a flat stone on the very top, a broad flat slab tipped a little to one side, like a hat worn at an angle. The other did not.
The stones of them were gray and gold and orange with lichen. Snow lay in every crack. At the foot of the one with the hat, somebody had left a small heap of pebbles, and a scrap of red cloth tied round a stone, faded almost to pink, and a little wooden thing that might once have been a bird.
Lyra had stopped in front of them. She stood with her head tipped back, looking up at the gap between their tops.
"Which way?" she said.
Oren came up and looked at both roads. He looked at them the way Corin had seen him look at doors, all through the city. Where they went. What they could hide. How quickly you could get out of them.
"Right," he said. "That one. It's the main road. It's walked. There'll be a village up it, or a farm. And the walls are good." He nodded at the left-hand way with his beard. "That one's not been walked since the autumn. We'd be breaking snow all afternoon, and with your leg—" He looked at Corin.
Lyra had taken something out of her coat. It was a piece of paper, folded small. She unfolded it with her gloved fingers and looked at it, frowning.
"He didn't give us a map," she said. "Kross. He only said it. On the step. I made Wren say it again, and I learned it." She did not read from the paper. Corin saw that there was nothing written on the paper. It was only a paper she had folded, the way her people folded things. She held it as if holding it helped her remember. "By the dyke road north. Past the reeds. Past the hills. North by the old road, and then north again, and you'll know it when you see it." She folded the paper up again. "North by the old road. That's all."
"They're both old," said Oren.
"I know they're both old."
"And they both go north. Near enough."
"I know, Oren."
They both turned to Corin. And both of them stopped.
Because Corin was not standing at the fork anymore.
He was a good few steps up the left-hand road.
He was standing in the drifted snow between the low, mossy, fallen walls, with his crutch sunk to the cross-piece in a drift, and his bad leg aching, and his good leg already lifted to take the next step. He looked down at his feet. He looked back at the two of them. He did not know how he had got there.
He had not decided. That was the thing. He went over it afterward, many times, and he was sure. He had not stood at the fork and looked at the two roads and thought, that one. He had not thought anything. He had been listening to the two of them talk, and looking at the scrap of faded red cloth at the foot of the cairn, and his feet had simply gone. Left. Up the narrow way. The way nobody had walked since the autumn. As if they had done it before, and did not need to be told.
"Corin?" said Lyra.
It was the first time that day she had said his name.
It went through him like warm water. He knew that voice. It was the one thing of her he had kept, and he had not heard it say his name since last night, and it said it now exactly as it did in his head: quick, and a little cross, and a little frightened under the cross.
"I don't know," he said. He meant it. "I don't know why. I just—this way."
He waited for one of them to argue.
Oren opened his mouth. He looked at Corin's face for a long moment. Then he shut his mouth again, and picked up his pack, and came across the fork, and stepped up into the snow of the left-hand road beside him.
"Well," said Oren. "It's north."
Lyra stood alone in front of the Two Sisters for a moment longer. She looked up at them again. Then she put the blank paper back inside her coat, and came after them.
Malakor, said Corin, inside.
There was a long pause.
Hm, said Malakor. Just that. Thin and far, through the wall.
Do you know why I did that?
Another pause. Longer.
No, said Malakor. Not why. And then, so faint that afterward Corin was not sure he had heard it at all: But it's the right way.
The snow on the left-hand road was deep. It came above Corin's ankles, and in places above his knees, where the wind had piled it against the wall. Every step was work. The crutch went down into it and found the hard road underneath only after a long, soft, sinking moment, so that every time he put his weight on it he did not know if it would hold. Oren went first, breaking the snow with his boots, kicking a path. Corin followed in the holes Oren left. Lyra came behind.
They did not talk. There was not breath to talk.
But once, about half an hour up the road, Corin stopped to rest against the wall, and turned and looked back down the valley, and saw the Two Sisters far below them, two small gray shapes leaning their heads together at the fork.
And he had the strangest feeling.
It was not a memory. He was sure it was not a memory. But for a moment, looking down at the two cairns from above, he felt very small. Small the way a child is small. He felt his hand in someone else's hand, a big dry old hand, and he felt that he was tired, and cold, and that his feet hurt, and that he was being pulled gently uphill by that hand, step by step, and that he did not mind. There were no words in it. No face. Only a hand, and the cold, and the hill.
Then it was gone.
He was a grown man with a crutch, leaning on a wall in the snow, and the girl had stopped beside him and was looking at his face.
"What is it?" she said.
"Nothing."
She looked at him a moment longer.
"Rule one," she said quietly.
He let out his breath.
"I don't know what it is," he said. "That's the truth. I don't know. My feet know this road. I don't."
She did not say anything to that. She only nodded, slowly, as if she were putting it somewhere safe. Then she went on up the road behind Oren, and after a moment, Corin followed her.
Breaking Snow
The left-hand road went up and up.
It did not zigzag, the way the sheep path had. It went straight at the hill, the way old roads do, as if the people who made it had had no time to go round anything. In places the walls on either side had fallen down altogether, and the road was only a long shallow dip in the snow between two lines of humps, and the snow lay in the dip so deep that Oren went into it to his thighs.
Oren did not complain. He did not say anything at all. He went first, and he broke the snow.
Corin had not known, before today, what that meant. He learned it now, watching from behind. It meant lifting one leg high, high as your hip, and pushing it forward into the white, and putting your weight on it, and feeling it go down, down, until it found something hard to stand on. Then dragging the other leg up out of the hole it was in, and lifting it high, and doing it again. Every step. With one arm in a sling, so that you could not use it to balance, and two packs on your back.
After a while Oren's breath began to come in long, harsh pulls, loud in the still air, with a little grunt at the end of each one. He did not slow down.
Corin followed in the holes he left.
That was easier, but it was not easy. The holes were deep and narrow, and the crutch did not fit in them. He had to put the crutch down beside the hole, on the unbroken snow, and the unbroken snow had a crust on top that would hold the crutch for a moment, a long trembling moment, and then break, so that the crutch plunged down and he lurched sideways after it. He fell three times in the first half hour. Each time he went down into the soft white beside the road, and each time it was the same: the cold, sudden and total, going into his collar and up his sleeves and into his mouth, and then the long, slow business of getting up again with a bad leg and no feeling in his fingers.
The first time, Oren came back for him.
The second time, the girl got there first.
She did not say anything. She came down into the snow beside him and got her shoulder under his arm, the way a soldier does for a wounded man, and she was stronger than she looked. She heaved, and he pushed with his good leg, and he came up out of the drift all at once, white from his hair to his boots, and stood swaying with his arm still round her shoulders.
For a moment neither of them moved.
He could feel her breathing, hard, against his side. He could feel how thin she was, under the big black coat, and how her shoulder was all bone. Her cap had come off in the snow. Her short hair was full of it. Her face was very close to his, and very red with cold and effort, and she was looking at him with an expression he could not read at all.
Then she let go of him, so suddenly that he nearly fell again, and bent and picked up his crutch out of the snow, and shoved it at him.
"You walk like a heron," she said. "Even when you fall over."
Then she went on up the road, fast, with her cap in her hand, beating the snow off it against her leg.
Corin stood and looked after her.
He knew that line. It was in the book. He had read it on Tuesday, in his own capitals: SHE SAYS I WALK LIKE A HERON. And under it, in her quick forward-leaning hand, the hand she did not have anymore: A heron just stands about. He had read it the way you read a joke in a book in another language, and understood the words, and not why it was funny.
He still did not know why it was funny. But he found he did not mind her saying it.
The third time he fell, he got up by himself, before either of them could reach him. It took a long time. He did it anyway.
They came at last to a place where the road leveled out a little, on a sort of step in the side of the hill, and the snow was not so deep, because the wind had blown most of it away. There was a stone there.
It stood by the side of the road, half buried, a single upright slab of gray rock about as high as his waist. It was not part of the wall. It had been set there on purpose, and it was old, older than the walls, he thought, because the walls had been built round it, bending a little out of their line to leave it room. Its top was rounded and smooth. Snow sat on it like a cap.
Oren stopped beside it to breathe. He leaned on it with his good hand.
Then he took his hand off it, quickly, and looked down.
"There's something on it," he said.
Corin came up and looked. Lyra came back down the road to look too.
Oren brushed the snow off the face of the stone with his sleeve. Under the snow, the stone was green-gray with lichen. And under the lichen, cut into the stone, very shallow and very worn, there was a shape.
It was a circle, with straight lines coming out of it all the way round.
"A sun," said Lyra.
Oren put his thumb on it. He traced the circle, slowly, and then one of the rays. His thumb was big and the carving was small, and he did it very carefully, the way a man touches something he is afraid of breaking.
"I've seen that before," he said slowly. "I've seen that somewhere." He frowned at it. "I don't know where."
Nobody said anything.
Corin looked at the sun on the stone, and then back down the road the way they had come, at the long line of holes they had left in the snow, going down, down, out of sight round the shoulder of the hill toward the Two Sisters. Then up the road the way they were going, where it went on over the next rise and out of sight, north.
The stone faced north. The sun on it faced north. Whoever had cut it had cut it so that you would see it if you were coming up the road from the fork. Coming up the left-hand way. The old way.
It was a sign. He was sure of it. It was a sign that said: this way. You are on the right road.
He did not know how he knew that. He did not know why it made his throat go tight.
"Come on," said Oren at last, and took his hand off the stone. "Light's going. We'll not find anything standing here."
They went on. Corin went last. As he passed the stone he put out his gray hand, without thinking, and laid it flat on the carved sun for a moment, the way you lay your hand on a dog's head as you pass it.
He could not feel the stone. His fingers could not feel anything. But he left his hand there for a breath anyway. Then he took it away and followed the others up the hill.
